content: CUB domain-containing protein 1 (CDCP1) is a protein encoded by the CDCP1 gene in humans. It is also referred to as CD318 (Cluster of Differentiation 318) or Trask (Transmembrane and associated with Src kinases). Alternative splicing of the CDCP1 gene results in the production of distinct isoforms of this protein. CDCP1, also known as Trask, does not appear to be essential for the development of mice. Adult mice that lack CDCP1 do not show any significant abnormalities in morphology, reproduction, or behavior when compared to wild-type mice. Histological analysis of various organ systems in these mice has not revealed any significant pathological changes or differences in tissue structure. CDCP1 functions as a ligand for CD6, a receptor molecule expressed on certain T-cells. This interaction may influence the migration and chemotaxis of these T-cells. Consequently, CDCP1 may play a role in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases, including encephalomyelitis, multiple sclerosis, and inflammatory arthritis. CDCP1 is a 140 kDa transmembrane glycoprotein. Its structure includes a large extracellular domain (ECD) containing two CUB domains and a smaller intracellular domain (ICD). The extracellular domain of CDCP1 can be cleaved by serine proteases at a specific site near Arg368, resulting in a truncated form of the protein that is approximately 80 kDa in size. The relative expression levels of the full-length 140 kDa protein (p140) and the truncated 80 kDa protein (p80) vary among different cell lines, depending on the activity of endogenous serine proteases. Under normal physiological conditions, CDCP1 is not cleaved in vivo. However, cleavage can occur during pathological processes such as tumorigenesis or tissue injury. The intracellular domain of CDCP1 contains five tyrosine residues: Y707, Y734, Y743, Y762, and Y806. Phosphorylation of these tyrosine residues is exclusively mediated by Src kinases and is influenced by the adherence state of the cells. In cultured cells, tyrosine phosphorylation of CDCP1 is observed when cells are induced to detach, such as through treatment with trypsin or EDTA, or during spontaneous detachment associated with mitosis. Cellular detachment and loss of anchorage are associated with CDCP1 phosphorylation, which occurs alongside the dephosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins. This process is consistent with the disassembly of focal adhesions. Conversely, during cellular attachment, CDCP1 is dephosphorylated, which allows for the phosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins. The anti-adhesion and anti-migratory effects of CDCP1 are mediated through its negative regulation of integrin receptors. Phosphorylation of CDCP1 has been observed in various cancers, including pre-invasive cancers, invasive tumors, and metastatic lesions. This suggests that CDCP1 phosphorylation may have clinical significance in the context of cancer progression and metastasis.
